introduction: The young King Henry V turns from his unruly past towards an ambitious claim to the French crown. Churchmen and nobles encourage him, while the Dauphin dismisses him as a frivolous prince. As England prepares an invasion, former tavern companions join an army whose commanders demand obedience and discipline. Across courts, camps and a threatened French town, the play tests royal resolve against ordinary fear, political calculation and the human consequences of a war pursued in the language of honour.

fullSynopsis.text: The Chorus asks the audience to imagine kingdoms and armies beyond the theatre's limits. In England, Canterbury and Ely fear a bill threatening Church property. They praise Henry's reformation, and Canterbury offers a large subsidy towards war in France. Asked to consider the bloodshed his advice may cause, he argues that Salic law does not bar Henry's inherited claim to the French crown. After considering England's defence during an invasion, Henry resolves to pursue it before receiving the Dauphin's mocking gift of tennis balls. He answers the insult with threats of war.

As England mobilizes, Henry exposes Cambridge, Scroop and Grey's conspiracy to kill him at Southampton. After they recommend severity towards a drunken offender, he reveals their own treason and sends them to death. In London, Bardolph mediates between Nym and Pistol, rivals over Quickly, now Pistol's wife. Their quarrel gives way to anxiety over Falstaff, whose broken heart they blame on the King. Quickly later describes his death, and the men depart for France with the Boy. At the French court, the Dauphin belittles Henry, while others fear his lineage and resolution; Exeter delivers the English demand for the crown.

The Chorus carries the fleet to Harfleur and reports Henry's rejection of a limited settlement. Henry urges his troops into the breach, while Fluellen drives the reluctant Pistol, Nym and Bardolph forward. The Boy condemns their cowardice and thieving and hopes for better service. Henry threatens Harfleur with massacre and sexual violence if resistance continues; when the unsupported governor yields, he orders mercy. Sickness drives the English towards Calais. Katharine, meanwhile, learns English from Alice. Pistol cannot persuade Fluellen to save Bardolph from execution for church robbery, and Henry endorses strict discipline and payment for supplies as the French prepare to intercept him.

On the night before Agincourt, French confidence contrasts with the English army's exhaustion. Moving through his camp in disguise, Henry hears soldiers question both the justice of his cause and his responsibility for their deaths. A quarrel with Williams ends in an exchange of gloves and a promised reckoning. Alone, Henry weighs the burdens of kingship and prays that his father's seizure of Richard's crown will not be visited on his army. In the morning, his Saint Crispin's Day speech makes their small numbers a promise of shared honour, and he again refuses ransom.

The French ranks collapse. Pistol extracts a ransom promise from a prisoner through the Boy's translation; the Boy reports Bardolph and Nym hanged and returns towards the poorly guarded baggage. Exeter recounts York and Suffolk's deaths. When the French regroup, Henry orders his soldiers to kill their prisoners. Afterwards, Gower reports the slaughter of the baggage boys and describes the prisoner killings as retaliation. Henry threatens further killings before Montjoy acknowledges English victory. The King attributes the astonishing disparity in reported losses to God, orders religious thanksgiving and prepares to return home.

Henry also settles his dispute with Williams by giving the soldier's glove to Fluellen with a false story about its French origin. Williams strikes Fluellen, then defends his earlier words on the ground that he could not recognize a disguised king. Henry rewards him and requires reconciliation. Later, Fluellen answers Pistol's insults to his Welsh leek by beating him and making him eat it. Pistol reports Doll dead and plans to return to England, steal, and pass his cudgel wounds off as battle scars. The Chorus compresses Henry's triumphant homecoming and subsequent return to France.

At the peace conference, Burgundy laments France's ruined land and society. Henry makes peace depend on acceptance of his demands, including Katharine's hand. Left with her and Alice, he presents himself as a plain soldier wooing across a language barrier; Katharine's agreement depends on her father's consent. The French accept the settlement, including Henry's designation as heir of France, and the parties prepare for marriage and mutual oaths. The epilogue qualifies this hopeful union: Henry's achievement will be brief, and under his infant successor Henry VI, France will be lost and England brought to bloodshed.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Canterbury and Ely discuss a parliamentary bill that would strip the Church of substantial wealth. Their admiration for Henry's apparent transformation accompanies a practical offer: Canterbury has proposed an exceptional clerical subsidy for his French enterprise. At court, Henry asks whether Salic law defeats his claim and warns the Archbishop against justifying a war dishonestly. Canterbury argues that the prohibition concerns German territory and that French kings themselves have inherited through women. The nobles encourage Henry to emulate his ancestors, while debate over Scotland establishes the need to defend England during his absence. Henry resolves to pursue the French crown. Only then does the Dauphin's embassy deliver tennis balls, mocking his youthful reputation. He promises to turn the joke into destructive war and orders the expedition's preparations to proceed.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: The Chorus describes England's preparations and reveals a French-funded plot against Henry before embarkation. In London, Nym resents Pistol's marriage to Quickly, but Bardolph negotiates a settlement between the quarrelling soldiers. News of Falstaff's illness interrupts them, and Quickly attributes his decline to the King's rejection. At Southampton, Henry first permits Cambridge, Scroop and Grey to urge punishment for a drunken insult, then exposes their own conspiracy. Their pleas do not avert the death sentence; Henry presents its discovery as divine support for his enterprise. Quickly subsequently reports Falstaff's death, recalling his last moments, and the men leave for France. There, Charles and the Constable caution against the Dauphin's contempt for Henry. Exeter demands recognition of the English title and warns of the suffering that refusal will bring.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: The Chorus imagines the fleet's crossing and reports a rejected offer of Katharine with limited territories. Before Harfleur, Henry rallies the assault, while his former companions shrink from danger and the Boy repudiates their thieving example. The Welsh Fluellen and Irish Macmorris quarrel over military practice while Gower and the Scottish Jamy try to keep their discussion civil. Henry threatens the town with atrocities if it resists; its governor, unable to obtain relief, surrenders, and Henry orders mercy and fortification. Katharine studies English with Alice as French nobles angrily prepare to challenge the invaders. On the march, Fluellen refuses Pistol's plea for Bardolph, condemned for stealing from a church. Henry supports punishment of such offenders and forbids mistreatment of civilians. Montjoy demands ransom, but Henry, admitting his troops' sickness and weakness, insists on passage towards Calais. French leaders await morning with boasts of easy victory.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: The Chorus contrasts the camps and celebrates Henry's encouraging presence. Disguised, he disputes royal responsibility with ordinary soldiers, quarrels with Williams, and later prays against inherited guilt for Richard's overthrow. His morning speech promises brotherhood and lasting honour. Battle overturns French confidence; Pistol secures a ransom promise, while Exeter reports York and Suffolk dead. Henry orders prisoners killed when the French regroup; Gower subsequently reports the baggage boys massacred and calls the prisoner killings retaliation. Montjoy concedes the English victory. Henry's glove trick makes Williams strike Fluellen before the King reveals their earlier encounter, accepts the soldier's defence and rewards him. Reports of enormous French losses beside few English deaths prompt thanksgiving and a prohibition on claiming glory apart from God. The army prepares to bury the dead and return by Calais.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: The Chorus carries Henry through a triumphant English welcome, stresses his refusal of personal trophies, and compresses intervening events before bringing him back to France. Fluellen punishes Pistol's mockery of the Welsh leek by beating him and forcing him to eat it. Pistol reports Doll's death and plans to survive through crime and fraudulent stories of military service. At the royal conference, Burgundy describes the devastation of French agriculture and civil life. Henry insists on his demands, sending the others to negotiate while he woos Katharine through imperfect English and French. She makes her consent depend on her father's approval, and Henry overrides her objection to a premarital kiss. The returning negotiators accept the settlement and his designation as France's heir. Marriage and reciprocal oaths are prepared as the courts hope for lasting peace.

framing.label: PROLOGUE
framing.summary: The Chorus asks pardon for presenting a vast war within the narrow theatre. It invites the audience to multiply a few actors into armies, imagine horses and the fields of France, and supply the movement across years and places through thought. This appeal establishes the Chorus as a guide whose narration repeatedly enlarges what the stage can show.

framing.label: EPILOGUE
framing.summary: The returning Chorus acknowledges how severely the play has compressed Henry's achievements. It praises his brief greatness, then looks beyond the settlement to his infant successor, Henry VI. Under the many hands governing that reign, France will be lost and England torn by bloodshed. The speech recalls those later histories as already familiar stage material, placing the apparent triumph within a longer cycle of loss.
